extraction_notes.note: Definition or algorithm: the pathwise construction of the Walsh process (excursions sent to edge k with probability w_k) is a recipe, but it serves to define the process W, so it is one definition node.

Definition or external theorem: the sentence applies Dynkin's formula for the generator at v, but what it introduces and what later nodes use is the exit time H^w_{v,epsilon}. Typed as that definition.

Remark or claim: each paragraph argues and concludes in one go (K_s is a stopping time; L^s is the local time of W^s; v is not a trap) with no separately stated result. RP11 is relied on later, in DP52.

The second proof of Theorem 3.2 is taken from 'With lemma 3.3 ...'. The earlier sentence that specializes (1.30) to the elastic process sits before Lemma 3.4 and is left outside the proof, so the lemma does not have to be nested in it.

In prose, the definitions of the killed processes and the claims that they are Brownian motions are interleaved. W^g is defined in the same sentence that asserts it is a Brownian motion, so it is a single definition node.

The defined-term check flags every 'Brownian motion'. Edges from DP7 go only to uses meaning a Brownian motion on the star graph; the many uses meaning standard or reflected Brownian motion on the line get none.

Left out: the introduction's survey and outline, the heuristic paragraph explaining why the vertex is 'sticky', convention sentences ('for the remainder of this section we choose a=c=0, w_k=b_k'), and the cited limits of g_{beta,gamma} as beta or gamma tend to 0.
The finishing step warns that the prose node starts mid-sentence. It starts right after a \vspace command at a real sentence start, so the warning is a false alarm.

nodes.name: Star graph (single vertex graph)
nodes.statement: The simplest metric graphs are \emph{star} or \emph{single vertex graphs}: They can be defined as a set having a finite collection of subsets isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_+$, called \emph{external edges}, where the points corresponding to the origin of $\mathbb{R}_+$ under these isomorphims are identified and form the \emph{vertex} of the graph.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and Preliminaries
differentia: having a finite collection of subsets isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_+$, called \emph{external edges}
nodes.statement_short: A star graph is finitely many copies of the half-line glued at their origins, which form the vertex.

nodes.name: Star graph $\mathcal{G}$ with vertex $v$ and edges $l_1,\dots,l_n$
nodes.statement: From now we shall consider a fixed star graph $\mathcal{G}$ with vertex $v$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ external edges $l_1$, \dots, $l_n$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Natural metric $d$ on $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{G}$ is equipped with the natural metric $d$ which is induced by the metric that each external edge inherits from being isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Open interior $\mathcal{G}^\circ$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{G}^\circ$ denotes the set $\mathcal{G}\setminus\{v\}$ which we also call --- by abuse of language --- the \emph{open interior} of $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Open edges $l_k^\circ$
nodes.statement: It is the disjoint union of $n$ copies $l_k^\circ$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, of the interval $(0,+\infty)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Local coordinates $(k,x)$
nodes.statement: Every $\xi\in\mathcal{G}^\circ$ is in one-to-one correspondence with its \emph{local coordinates} $(k,x)$, where $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ is the index of the edge $\xi$ belongs to, and $x>0$ denotes the distance of $\xi$ to $v$. For simplicity we shall often write $\xi=(k,x)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Brownian motion on a star graph
nodes.statement: A \emph{Brownian motion} $X=(X_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ on $\mathcal{G}$ is a diffusion process on $\mathcal{G}$, such that $X$ with absorption at $v$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the half line $\mathbb{R}_+$ with absorption at the origin.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
differentia: $X$ with absorption at $v$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the half line $\mathbb{R}_+$ with absorption at the origin
nodes.statement_short: A Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ is a diffusion that, absorbed at $v$, is a half-line Brownian motion absorbed at 0.
nodes.label: def_BM

nodes.name: Diffusion process and usual conditions
nodes.statement: By a diffusion process we mean a strong Markov process (e.g., in the sense of~\cite{BlGe68}), which a.s.\ has c\`adl\`ag paths and a.s.\ the paths are continuous on $[0,\zeta)$, where $\zeta$ is its lifetime. Moreover, in definition~\ref{def_BM} we have --- as we shall usually do without any danger of confusion --- identified the external leg $l_k$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, on which the process starts with the corresponding copy of $\mathbb{R}_+$. Throughout we shall assume without loss of generality that the filtration of a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ satisfies the ``usual conditions'', i.e., it is right continuous and complete relative to the underlying family $(P_\xi,\,\xi\in\mathcal{G})$ of probability measures.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Diffusion = strong Markov, cadlag, continuous before lifetime; filtrations satisfy the usual conditions.
nodes.label: rem_BM

nodes.name: Banach space $C_0(\mathcal{G})$
nodes.statement: $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ denotes the Banach space of continuous functions on $\mathcal{G}$ which vanish at infinity equipped with the sup-norm.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
differentia: continuous functions on $\mathcal{G}$ which vanish at infinity

nodes.name: Function space $C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$
nodes.statement: Define $\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ as the subspace of $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ consisting of those functions $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ which are twice continuously differentiable on $\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ$, such that $f''$ extends from $\mathcal{G}^\circ$ to $\mathcal{G}$ as a function in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
differentia: $f''$ extends from $\mathcal{G}^\circ$ to $\mathcal{G}$ as a function in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$

nodes.name: Directional derivatives of $C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ functions at the vertex
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$, $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$. Then the limit of $f'(\xi)$ as $\xi$ converges to $v$ along the open edge $l_k^\circ$ exists. The directional derivatives $f^{(i)}(v_k)$, $i=1$, $2$, of first and second order of $f$ at the vertex $v$ in direction of the edge $l_k$ exist, and the equalities \begin{equation*} f^{(i)}(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k^\circ} f^{(i)}(\xi),\qquad i=1,\,2, \end{equation*} hold true. Moreover, $f'$ vanishes at infinity.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
conclusions: the limit of $f'(\xi)$ as $\xi$ converges to $v$ along the open edge $l_k^\circ$ exists
$f'$ vanishes at infinity
nodes.statement_short: For $f\in C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$, one-sided first and second derivatives at $v$ along each edge exist as limits, and $f'$ vanishes at infinity.
nodes.label: lemC02

nodes.name: Second derivative at the vertex is edge independent
nodes.statement: By definition we have that for every $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ and all $j$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, $f''(v_j) = f''(v_k)$, and henceforth we shall simply write $f''(v)$ for this quantity. On the other hand, in general $f'(v_j)\ne f'(v_k)$ for $j\ne k$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.label: remC02

nodes.name: Every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
conclusions: every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the Feller property
nodes.statement: A convenient way to prove this is to show that its resolvent maps $C_0(\mathcal{G})$ into itself by arguments similar to those in~\cite[Section~3.6]{ItMc74}, and to observe that the path properties imply for all $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $P_t f(\xi)$ converges to $f(\xi)$ as $t$ decreases to $0$, where $(P_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ denotes the semigroup generated by the Brownian motion. Then one can use well-known arguments (for example, a complete proof can be found in~\cite{NFSG}) to conclude the Feller property in its usual form, e.g., \cite{ReYo91}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Show the resolvent preserves $C_0(\mathcal{G})$ as in Ito-McKean and use pointwise continuity at $t=0$, then cite standard arguments.

nodes.name: Feller's theorem for star graphs
nodes.statement: Assume that $X$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$. Then there exist constants $a$, $b_k$, $c\in[0,1]$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, with \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} a + c + \sum_{k=1}^n b_k = 1,\quad a\ne 1, \end{equation} such that the domain $\mathcal{D}(A)$ of the generator $A$ of $X$ in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ consists exactly of those $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ for which \begin{equation} a f(v) + \frac{c}{2}\,f''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} \end{subequations} holds true. Moreover, for $f\in\mathcal{D}(A)$, $Af = 1/2 f''$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.origin_citation: Feller; Knight 1981 (Thm 6.2); Kostrykin, Potthoff, Schrader (BMMG, Thm 1.3)
conclusions: there exist constants $a$, $b_k$, $c\in[0,1]$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$
for $f\in\mathcal{D}(A)$, $Af = 1/2 f''$
nodes.statement_short: The generator of any Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ is $\frac12 f''$ on $C_0^2$ functions satisfying a Wentzell vertex condition $af(v)+\frac c2 f''(v)=\sum b_k f'(v_k)$.
nodes.label: thm_Feller

nodes.name: Normalization of boundary parameters
nodes.statement: a + c + \sum_{k=1}^n b_k = 1,\quad a\ne 1,
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.label: eq1.1a

nodes.name: Wentzell boundary condition at the vertex
nodes.statement: a f(v) + \frac{c}{2}\,f''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k)
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.label: eq1.1b

nodes.name: Proof of Feller's theorem by reference
nodes.statement: The proof in~\cite{Kn81} for the case where $\mathcal{G}$ has only one external edge, i.e., $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$, is readily modified for a general star graph $\mathcal{G}$. On the other hand, theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} also follows from Feller's theorem in the case of a general metric graph~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{BMMG}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: By reference: Knight's half-line proof adapts, or specialize the metric-graph Feller theorem of BMMG.

nodes.name: Standard Brownian motion $B$ with family $(Q_x)$
nodes.statement: Let $(Q_x,\,x\in\mathbb{R})$ denote a family of probability measures on a measurable space $(\Omega',\mathcal{A}')$, and let $B=(B_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ denote a standard Brownian motion defined on $(\Omega',\mathcal{A}')$ with $Q_x(B_0=x)=1$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Shift operator $\theta$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we may suppose that there is a shift operator $\theta: \mathbb{R}_+\times\Omega \to\Omega$, such that for all $s$, $t\ge 0$, $B_s\comp\theta_t=B_{s+t}$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Filtration $\mathcal{J}$
nodes.statement: We shall always understand the Brownian family $(B, (Q_x,\,x\in\mathbb{R}))$ to be equipped with a filtration $\mathcal{J}=(\mathcal{J}_t,\,t\ge 0)$ which is right continuous and complete for the family $(Q_x,\,x\in\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Hitting time $H^B_A$
nodes.statement: For any $A\subset\mathbb{R}$, we denote by $H^B_A$ the hitting time of $A$ by $B$, \begin{equation} H^B_A = \inf\{t>0,\,B_t\in A\}, \end{equation} and we note that for all $A$ belonging to the Borel $\sigma$--algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ of $\mathbb{R}$, $H^B_A$ is a stopping time with respect to $\mathcal{J}$ (e.g., \cite[Theorem~III.2.17]{ReYo91}).
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Hitting time $H^B_A$
nodes.statement: H^B_A = \inf\{t>0,\,B_t\in A\},
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.2

nodes.name: Hitting time of a point $H^B_x$
nodes.statement: In the case where $A=\{x\}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, we also simply write $H^B_x$ for $H^B_{\{x\}}$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Hitting time density and Laplace transform for Brownian motion
nodes.statement: Let $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then we have (e.g., \cite[Sect.~1.7]{ItMc74}, \cite[Sect.~2.6]{KaSh91}, \cite[Sect.'s~II.3, III.3]{ReYo91}) \begin{equation} Q_0(H^B_x\in dt) = Q_x(H^B_0\in dt) = \frac{|x|}{t}\,g(t,x)\,dt,\qquad t>0, \end{equation} where $g$ is the Gau{\ss}-kernel \begin{equation} g(t,x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-x^2/2t},\qquad t>0,\,x\in\mathbb{R}, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\lambda H^B_x}\bigr) = E^Q_x\bigl(e^{-\lambda H^B_0}\bigr) = e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} |x|},\qquad \lambda>0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.origin_citation: Ito & McKean 1974; Karatzas & Shreve 1991; Revuz & Yor 1991
nodes.statement_short: Density $\frac{|x|}{t}g(t,x)$ of the hitting time of $x$ from 0 and its Laplace transform $e^{-\sqrt{2\lambda}|x|}$; $g$ is the Gauss kernel.

nodes.name: Density of Brownian hitting time
nodes.statement: Q_0(H^B_x\in dt) = Q_x(H^B_0\in dt) = \frac{|x|}{t}\,g(t,x)\,dt,\qquad t>0,
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.3

nodes.name: Gauss kernel $g(t,x)$
nodes.statement: g(t,x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-x^2/2t},\qquad t>0,\,x\in\mathbb{R},
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.4

nodes.name: Laplace transform of Brownian hitting time
nodes.statement: E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\lambda H^B_x}\bigr) = E^Q_x\bigl(e^{-\lambda H^B_0}\bigr) = e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} |x|},\qquad \lambda>0.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.5

nodes.name: Expected exit time of an interval
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $a<x<b$ the law of $H^B_{\{a,b\}}$ under $Q_x$ is well-known (e.g., \cite[Problem~6, Sect.~1.7]{ItMc74}), and its expectation is given by \begin{equation} E^Q_x\bigl(H^B_{\{a,b\}}\bigr) = (x-a)(b-x). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
conclusions: its expectation is given by
nodes.statement_short: For $a<x<b$, the expected exit time of $(a,b)$ by Brownian motion from $x$ is $(x-a)(b-x)$.

nodes.name: Expected exit time formula
nodes.statement: E^Q_x\bigl(H^B_{\{a,b\}}\bigr) = (x-a)(b-x).
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.6

nodes.name: Local time $L^B$ of Brownian motion at zero
nodes.statement: Denote by $L^B=(L^B_t,\,t\ge 0)$ the local time of $B$ at zero, where we choose the normalization as in, e.g., \cite{ReYo91} (and which thus differs by a factor $2$ from the one used in, e.g., \cite{IkWa89, KaSh91}): for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $P_x$--a.s.\ \begin{equation} L^B_t = \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0}\,\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\, \lambda\bigl(\bigl\{s\le t,\,|B_s|\le \epsilon\bigr\}\bigr), \qquad t\ge 0, \end{equation} and here $\lambda$ denotes the Lebesgue measure.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.statement_short: $L^B$ is Brownian local time at 0, normalized as occupation density $\lim (2\epsilon)^{-1}|\{s\le t: |B_s|\le\epsilon\}|$.

nodes.name: Local time as occupation limit
nodes.statement: L^B_t = \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0}\,\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\, \lambda\bigl(\bigl\{s\le t,\,|B_s|\le \epsilon\bigr\}\bigr), \qquad t\ge 0,
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.7

nodes.name: $\alpha$-potential of $L^B$
nodes.statement: u^\alpha_{L^B}(x) = E_x\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha t}\,dL^B_t\Bigr) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\alpha}}\,e^{-\sqrt{2\alpha}|x|},\qquad \alpha>0,\,x\in\mathbb{R},
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.7a

nodes.name: Local time as integral of Dirac delta
nodes.statement: L^B_t = \int_0^t \delta_0(B_s)\,ds,
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.8

nodes.name: Additivity of $L^B$
nodes.statement: L^B_{t+s} = L^B_t + L^B_s\comp\theta_t,\qquad s,t\in\mathbb{R}_+.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.label: eq1.9

nodes.name: Joint law of $|B_t|$ and $L_t$
nodes.statement: The joint law of $|B_t|$ and $L_t$, $t>0$, under $Q_0$ is given by \begin{equation} Q_0\bigl(|B_t|\in dx,\,L^B_t\in dy\bigr) = 2\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}\,e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}\,dx\,dy,\qquad x,y\ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
conclusions: The joint law of $|B_t|$ and $L_t$
nodes.statement_short: Joint density of $(|B_t|,L^B_t)$ under $Q_0$ is $2\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}$.
nodes.label: lem1.1

nodes.name: Joint density of $(|B_t|,L^B_t)$
nodes.statement: Q_0\bigl(|B_t|\in dx,\,L^B_t\in dy\bigr) = 2\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}\,e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}\,dx\,dy,\qquad x,y\ge 0.

nodes.name: Argument that $\hat X$ is a Brownian motion
nodes.statement: It is clear that $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ has a.s.\ right continuous paths which admit left limits, and that its paths on $[0,\zeta_\beta)$ are equal to those of $X$, and thus are continuous on this random time interval. Moreover, it is obvious that for every $\xi\in\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ$, we have $P_\xi(\zeta_\beta \ge H_v)=1$. nodes.statement: Altogether we have proved that --- under the hypothesis that $L$ is a PCHAF, which will be argued below in all cases that we consider --- $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.11
nodes.statement: For $\lambda>0$, $f\in B(\mathcal{G})$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$ \begin{align*} \ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda f(\xi) &= \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\Bigl(\int_0^{\zeta_\beta} e^{-\lambda t} f(X_t)\,dt\Bigr)\\ &= R_\lambda f(\xi) - \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda\zeta_\beta} \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\,f\bigl(X_{t+\zeta_\beta}\bigr)\,dt\Bigr). \end{align*} By construction, the last expectation value is equal to \begin{equation*} \beta\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta s}\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr)\,dt\,ds, \end{equation*} where we used Fubini's theorem. Consider the expectation value under the integrals, and recall that for fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s$ is an $\mathcal{F}$--stopping time, while $X$ is strongly Markovian relative to $\mathcal{F}$. Hence we can compute as follows \begin{align*} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr) &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,E_\xi\Bigl(f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{K_s}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,E_{X(K_s)}\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr)\,E_v\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the fact that a.s.\ $X(K_s)=v$. So far we have established \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda f(\xi) = R_\lambda f(\xi) - \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr)\,R_\lambda f(v). \end{equation*} In order to compute the expectation value on the right hand side, we first remark that because $L$ is zero until $X$ hits the vertex for the first time, we find that for given $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s\ge H_v$, and therefore $K_s = H_v + K_s\comp \theta_{H_v}$. Hence, and again by the strong Markov property, \begin{align*} E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr) &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,e^{-\lambda K_s\comp H_v}\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s\comp H_v}\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{H_v}\bigr)\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\bigr) E_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr), \end{align*} Integrating the last identity against the exponential law in the variable $s$, we find with formula~\eqref{eq1.14} \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda\zeta_\beta}\bigr) = e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr), \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.

nodes.statement_short: Strong Markov property at the stopping times $K_s$ and $H_v$, integrated against the exponential law of $S$ via Fubini.

nodes.name: Strong Markov at $K_s$
nodes.statement: Consider the expectation value under the integrals, and recall that for fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s$ is an $\mathcal{F}$--stopping time, while $X$ is strongly Markovian relative to $\mathcal{F}$. nodes.name: Decompose $K_s$ at $H_v$
nodes.statement: In order to compute the expectation value on the right hand side, we first remark that because $L$ is zero until $X$ hits the vertex for the first time, we find that for given $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s\ge H_v$, and therefore $K_s = H_v + K_s\comp \theta_{H_v}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, and again by the strong Markov property, \begin{align*} E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr) &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,e^{-\lambda K_s\comp H_v}\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s\comp H_v}\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{H_v}\bigr)\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\bigr) E_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr), \end{align*} Integrating the last identity against the exponential law in the variable $s$, we find with formula~\eqref{eq1.14} \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda\zeta_\beta}\bigr) = e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr), \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.

nodes.name: Walsh process
nodes.statement: The most basic process --- which on a single vertex graph plays the same role as a reflected Brownian motion on the half line --- is the well-known \emph{Walsh process}, which we denote by $W=(W_t,\,t\ge 0)$.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process

nodes.name: Pathwise construction of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the paths of the standard Brownian motion $B=(B_t,\,t\ge 0)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and its associated reflected Brownian motion $|B|=(|B_t|,\,t\ge 0)$, where $|\,\cdot\,|$ denotes absolute value. Let $Z=\{t\ge 0,\,B_t=0\}$. Then its complement $Z^c$ is open, and hence it is the pairwise disjoint union of a countable family of \emph{excursion intervals} $I_j = (t_j, t_{j+1})$, $j\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $R=(R_j,\,j\in\mathbb{N})$ be an independent sequence of identically distributed random variables, independent of $B$, with values in $\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$ such that $R_j$, $j\in\mathbb{N}$, takes the value $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$ with probability $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\sum_k w_k =1$. Now define $W_t = v$ if $t\in Z$, and if $t\in I_j$, and $R_j = k$ set $W_t = (k, |B_t|)$. In other words, when starting at $\xi\in\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ$, the process moves as a Brownian motion on the edge containing $\xi$ until it hits the vertex at time $H_v$, and then $W$ performs Brownian excursions from the vertex $v$ into the edges $l_k$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$, whereby the edge $l_k$ is selected with probability $w_k$.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Reflect a Brownian motion and send each excursion from 0 into edge $k$ independently with probability $w_k$.

nodes.name: Scattering matrix of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: The matrix $\ensuremath S^w=\bigl(\ensuremath S^w_{km},\,k,m = 1,\dotsc,n\bigr)$ is the \emph{scattering matrix} as defined in quantum mechanics. We briefly recall its construction in the present context, for more details the interested reader is referred to~\cite{KoSc99}. $\ensuremath S^w$ is obtained from the boundary conditions at the vertex $v$ in the following way. Consider a function $f$ on $\mathcal{G}$ which is continuously differentiable in $\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ=\mathcal{G}\setminus\{v\}$, and such that for all $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$ the limits \begin{align*} F_k &= f(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\ensuremath^\circ} f(\xi)\\ F'_k &= f'(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\ensuremath^\circ} f'(\xi) \end{align*} exist. Define two column vectors $F$, $F'\in\mathbb{C}^n$, having the components $F_k$ and $F'_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, respectively. Furthermore, consider boundary conditions of the following form \begin{equation} A F + B F' =0, \end{equation} where $A$ and $B$ are complex $n\times n$ matrices. The \emph{on-shell scattering matrix at energy $E>0$} is defined as \begin{equation} S_{A,B}(E) = - (A+i\sqrt{E}B)^{-1}(A-i\sqrt{E}B), \end{equation} which exists and is unitary, provided the $n\times 2n$ matrix $(A,B)$ has maximal rank (i.e., rank $n$) and $AB^\dagger$ is hermitian. These requirements for $A$ and $B$ guarantee that the corresponding Laplace operator is self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ (with Lebesgue measure). Observe that under these conditions the boundary conditions~\eqref{bc} are equivalent to any boundary conditions of the form $CAF+CBF'=0$ where $C$ is invertible. Also $S_{CA, CB}(E) = S_{A,B}(E)$ holds true. For the Walsh process at hand, concrete choices for $A$ and $B$ are given by \begin{equation*} A^w=\begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1 \end{pmatrix},\ B^w=\begin{pmatrix} b_1&b_2&b_3&\ldots&b_{n-1}&b_n\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation*} Then~\eqref{bc} is the condition that $f$ is actually continuous at the vertex $v$, i.e., $f(v_k)=f(v_m)$, $k$, $m=1,\dotsc,n$, and that~\eqref{eq2.2} is valid (with $w_k=b_k$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$). Obviously, $(A^w, B^w)$ has maximal rank. However, $A^w (B^w)^\dagger$ is hermitian if and only if all $b_k$ are equal (i.e., $b_k = 1/n$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$). Nevertheless, \eqref{SE} exists also in the non-hermitian case, and $S_{A^w, B^w}(E)=S^w$ holds for all $E>0$ due to the relations $A^w S^w = - A^w$, and $B^w S^w = B^w$. In addition, the following relations are valid: \begin{align} \ensuremath S^w &= \bigl(\ensuremath S^w\bigr)^{-1}, \\ \det \ensuremath S^w &= (-1)^{n+1}. \end{align} Furthermore, $S^w$ is a contraction, and the associated Laplace operator is m-dissipative on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ since trivially $\text{Im}(AB^\dagger)=0$, cf.\ Theorem~2.5 in~\cite{KoPo09c}. When all $b_k$ are equal, such that $A^w(B^w)^\dag=0$, then $S^w$ is an involutive, orthogonal matrix of the form \begin{equation} S^w = - \1 + 2P_n. \end{equation} $P_n$ is the matrix whose entries are equal to $1/n$. $P_n$ is a real orthogonal projection, that is $P_n = P_n^\dag = P_n^t = P_n^2$. It is also of rank $1$, that is $\dim \text{Ran} P_n = 1$. The relation~\eqref{eq2.4b} giving the resolvent in terms of the scattering matrix is actually valid in the more general context of arbitrary metric graphs and boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc}, see~\cite{KoSc06, KoPo09c}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: We may consider the Walsh process $W$ as being pathwise constructed from a standard Brownian motion $B$ on the real line as in the previous section, and we shall use the notations and conventions from there. Then it is clear that under $P_v$ and under $\ensuremath{\hat P}_v$, $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ has the same law as the hitting time of the point $\epsilon$ in $\mathbb{R}_+$ by the reflecting Brownian motion $|B|$ under $Q_0$, that is, as $H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}}$ of the Brownian motion $B$ itself under $Q_0$. Let $K^w$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^w$. For fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$ we get \begin{equation*} \{K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\} = \{L^w(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})>s\}. \end{equation*} Hence \begin{align*} P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) &= P_v\bigl(L^w(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})>s\bigr)\\ &= Q_0\bigl(L^B(H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}})>s\bigr). \end{align*} In appendix~B of~\cite{BMMG0} is shown with the method in~\cite[Section~6.4]{KaSh91} that under $Q_0$ the random variable $L^B(H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}})$ is exponentially distributed with mean $\epsilon$. So we find \begin{equation*} P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) = e^{-s/\epsilon}. \end{equation*} We integrate this relation against the exponential law with rate $\beta$ in the variable $s$, and obtain \begin{align*} \ensuremath{\hat P}_v\bigl(\zeta_{\beta,0}>\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) &= 1 - \beta\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta s}\,P_v\bigl(K^W_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)\,ds\\ &= \frac{1}{1+\epsilon\beta}. \end{align*} We used the fact that due to the continuity of the paths of $W$ we have $\zeta_{\beta,0}\ne \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$.

nodes.statement: R^e_\lambda f(\xi) = \ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(\xi) - \frac{\beta}{\beta + \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_\lambda(\xi)\, \ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(v).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.5

nodes.name: Walsh boundary condition
nodes.statement: Note that $\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f$ is in the domain of the generator of the Walsh process, and therefore satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq2.2}: \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\bigl(\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = 0. \end{equation*} On the other hand, we obviously have $e_\lambda'(v_k) = -\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}$ for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: $R^w_\lambda f$ satisfies the Walsh condition (2.2) and $e_\lambda'(v_k)=-\sqrt{2\lambda}$.

nodes.name: Derivative and value at $v$
nodes.statement: Thus with $\sum_{k=1}^n w_k =1$ we find, \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \bigl(R^e_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = \beta\,\frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(v), \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\sum w_k(R^e_\lambda f)'(v_k)$ and $R^e_\lambda f(v)$.

nodes.name: Elastic condition for the resolvent
nodes.statement: The last two equations show that for all $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $\lambda>0$, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \bigl(R^e_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = \beta\, R^e_\lambda f(v). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: $\sum w_k(R^e_\lambda f)'(v_k)=\beta R^e_\lambda f(v)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since for every $\lambda>0$, $R^e_\lambda$ maps $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ onto the domain of the generator of $\ensuremath W^e$, we have another proof of theorem~\ref{thm3.2}.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: The resolvent maps onto the domain of the generator.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: Upon insertion of the expressions for the resolvent kernels of the Walsh process, equations~\eqref{eq2.3}, and \eqref{eq2.4}, with the same notation as in lemma~\ref{lem2.3} we immediately obtain the following result:
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Insert the Walsh resolvent kernels (2.3), (2.4) into (3.5).

nodes.name: Resolvent kernel of the elastic Walsh process
nodes.statement: For $\lambda>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\mathcal{G}$ the resolvent kernel of the elastic Walsh process $\ensuremath W^e$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{align} \ensuremath r^e_\lambda(\xi,\eta) &= r^D_\lambda(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\,2w_m \,\frac{1}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_{\lambda,m}(\eta) \\ &= r_\lambda(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\,\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) \,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\, e_{\lambda,m}(\eta), \end{align} with the scattering matrix $\ensuremath S^e$ \begin{equation} \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) = 2\,\frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,w_m - \delta_{km},\qquad \lambda>0,\,k,m\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Elastic resolvent kernel with $\lambda$-dependent scattering matrix $S^e_{km}=2\frac{\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\sqrt{2\lambda}}w_m-\delta_{km}$.
nodes.label: lem3.4

nodes.name: Elastic Walsh resolvent kernel
nodes.statement: \ensuremath r^e_\lambda(\xi,\eta) &= r^D_\lambda(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\,2w_m \,\frac{1}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_{\lambda,m}(\eta) \\ &= r_\lambda(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\,\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) \,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\, e_{\lambda,m}(\eta),
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.6a

nodes.name: Elastic scattering matrix
nodes.statement: \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) = 2\,\frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,w_m - \delta_{km},\qquad \lambda>0,\,k,m\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.6c

nodes.name: Elastic scattering matrix and recovery of parameters
nodes.statement: Note that in contrast to the case of the Walsh process, this time the scattering matrix is not constant with respect to $\lambda>0$. Also, when $\beta=0$, formula~\eqref{eq2.4c} is recovered, as it should be. In analogy with the discussion in remark~\ref{rem2.4}, the boundary conditions for the elastic Walsh process is given by the matrices \begin{equation*} A^e = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0&\ldots&0&\beta\\ 1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1 \end{pmatrix},\ B^e=\begin{pmatrix} w_1&w_2&w_3&\ldots&w_{n-1}&w_n\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation*} such that \begin{align*} \ensuremath S^e(\lambda) &= S_{A^e,B^e}(E=-2\lambda)\\ &= - (A^e+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} B^e)^{-1}\,(A^e-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} B^e). \end{align*} Observe that for $k$, $m\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ the matrix element $\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)$ of the scattering matrix is obtained from the resolvent kernel as \begin{equation*} \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) = \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\lim_{\xi,\,\eta\to v}\bigl(\ensuremath r^e_\lambda(\xi,\eta) - r_\lambda(\xi,\eta)\bigr), \end{equation*} where the limit on the right hand side is taken in such a way that $\xi$, $\eta$ converge to $v$ along the edges $l_k$, $l_m$ respectively. $\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)$ in turn fixes the data $w_m$ and $\beta$, e.g., via the behavior for large $\lambda$, that is from the behavior at ``large energies'' \begin{equation*} w_m = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\delta_{km} + \lim_{\lambda'\ensuremath\uparrow\infty} \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda')\bigr), \quad \text{for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}, \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \beta = \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\Bigl(\frac{\delta_{km}+\lim_{\lambda'\ensuremath\uparrow\infty}\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda')} {\delta_{km}+\ensuremath S^e_{mm}(\lambda)}-1\Bigr),\quad \text{for all $\lambda$, and all $k$, $m\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}. \end{equation*} Alternatively, the data can be obtained from the small $\lambda$ behavior, that is the threshold behavior, of the scattering matrix, since from \begin{equation*} \frac{w_m}{\beta} = \lim_{\lambda \ensuremath\downarrow 0} \frac{1}{2\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\bigl(\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)+\delta_{km}\bigr) \qquad \text{for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}, \end{equation*} we obtain \begin{equation*} \beta^{-1} = \frac{1}{2\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^n\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)+1\Bigr) \qquad \text{for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}, \end{equation*} and therefore \begin{equation*} w_m = \frac{\lim_{\lambda\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \lambda^{-1/2}\bigl(\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)+\delta_{km}\bigr)} {\lim_{\lambda\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \lambda^{-1/2}\Bigl(\sum_m\ensuremath S^e_{k'm}(\lambda)+1\Bigr)} \qquad \text{for all $k$, $k'\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}. \end{equation*} Furthermore we remark that in the context of quantum mechanics in the self-adjoint case $w_k=1/n$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, the boundary conditions of the elastic Walsh process are interpreted as the presence of a $\delta$--potential of strength $\beta$ at the vertex.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: $S^e(\lambda)$ depends on $\lambda$, comes from boundary matrices $A^e,B^e$, and determines $w_m$ and $\beta$ from its high- or low-energy behaviour.
nodes.label: rem3.5

nodes.name: Two inverse Laplace transforms
nodes.statement: \frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\quad &\mathop{\longrightarrow}^{\mathcal{L}^{-1}}\quad \epsilon_0(dt) - \beta\Bigl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}-\frac{\beta}{2}e^{\beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr)\Bigr)\,dt,\\ \frac{1}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} x}\quad &\mathop{\longrightarrow}^{\mathcal{L}^{-1}}\quad g(t,x) - \frac{\beta}{2}\,e^{\beta x+ \beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.7

nodes.name: Inverse Laplace transform of the elastic scattering matrix
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \ensuremath s^e_{km}(dt) = (2w_m-\delta_{km})\,\epsilon_0(dt) &- 2w_m\beta\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,dt\\ & + w_m\beta^2 e^{\beta^2t/2}\,\mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr)\,dt, \end{split}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.9

nodes.name: Kernel $g_{\beta,0}$
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $t>0$, $x\ge 0$, let us introduce \begin{equation} g_{\beta,0}(t,x) = g(t,x) - \frac{\beta}{2}\,e^{\beta x+ \beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process

nodes.name: Definition of $g_{\beta,0}$
nodes.statement: g_{\beta,0}(t,x) = g(t,x) - \frac{\beta}{2}\,e^{\beta x+ \beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.10

nodes.name: Transition density of the elastic Walsh process
nodes.statement: For $t>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\mathcal{G}$, the transition density $\ensuremath p^e$ of the elastic Walsh process is given by \begin{equation} \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\,g_{\beta,0}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta), \end{equation} and alternatively by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n &\onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(\int_0^t P_\xi(\ensuremath H^w_v\in ds)\\ &\times \Bigl(\ensuremath s^e_{km}*g\bigl(\cdot,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\Bigr)(t-s)\, \Bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $*$ denotes convolution.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Elastic Walsh transition density = Dirichlet kernel plus $2w_m g_{\beta,0}(t,d_v)$ vertex terms.
nodes.label: lem3.6

nodes.name: Elastic transition density
nodes.statement: \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\,g_{\beta,0}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta),
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.11

nodes.name: Elastic density via scattering measure
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n &\onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(\int_0^t P_\xi(\ensuremath H^w_v\in ds)\\ &\times \Bigl(\ensuremath s^e_{km}*g\bigl(\cdot,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\Bigr)(t-s)\, \Bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \end{split}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.12

nodes.name: Time change $\tau$
nodes.statement: For $\gamma\ge 0$ introduce a new time scale $\tau$ by \begin{equation} \tau^{-1}: t\mapsto t + \gamma L^w_t, \qquad t\ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Inverse time change $\tau^{-1}$
nodes.statement: \tau^{-1}: t\mapsto t + \gamma L^w_t, \qquad t\ge 0.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.1

nodes.name: Additivity of the time change
nodes.statement: For all $s$, $t\ge 0$, a.s.\ the following formula holds true \begin{equation} \tau(s+t) = \tau(s) + \tau(t)\comp \theta_{\tau(s)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: lem4.1

nodes.name: Additivity of $\tau$
nodes.statement: \tau(s+t) = \tau(s) + \tau(t)\comp \theta_{\tau(s)}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.2

nodes.name: Time-changed filtration $\mathcal{F}^s$
nodes.statement: It is easily checked that for every $t\ge 0$, $\tau(t)$ is an $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$--stopping time, and since $\tau$ is increasing, we obtain the subfiltration $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s = (\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t,\,t\ge 0)$ of $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$ defined by $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t = \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{\tau(t)}$, $t\in\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Walsh process with sticky vertex
nodes.statement: Define a stochastic process $\ensuremath W^s$ on $\mathcal{G}$, called \emph{Walsh process with sticky vertex}, by \begin{equation} \ensuremath W^s_t = W_{\tau(t)},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}_+. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: The sticky Walsh process is the Walsh process time-changed by the inverse of $t+\gamma L^w_t$.

nodes.name: Sticky Walsh process $W^s_t=W_{\tau(t)}$
nodes.statement: \ensuremath W^s_t = W_{\tau(t)},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}_+.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.3

nodes.name: Shift operators $\theta^s$
nodes.statement: Set $\theta^s_t = \theta_{\tau(t)}$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Shift property of $W^s$
nodes.statement: W^s_s\comp\theta^s_t = W^s_{s+t},\qquad s,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: sshift

nodes.name: Strong Markov property of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: Next we show the strong Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ relative to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$ following the argument briefly sketched in section~6.2 of~\cite{Kn81} for the case $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$. First we prove the simple Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$. To this end, let $s$, $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. Then we get with~\eqref{sshift} \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+s}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_s\comp\theta^s_t\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(s)}\comp\theta_{\tau(t)}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{\tau(t)}\bigr)\\ &= P_{W_{\tau(t)}} \bigl(W_{\tau(s)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_{\ensuremath W^s_t}\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_s\in C\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the strong Markov property of $W$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$. As a next step we prove that $\ensuremath W^s$ has the strong Markov property for its hitting time $H^s_v$ of the vertex. By construction, $\ensuremath W^s$ and $W$ have the same paths up to the hitting time of the vertex, and in particular $H^s_v$ is also the hitting time of the vertex by $W$, that is, $H^s_v=H_v$. Moreover, since $L^w(H_v)=0$, we get that $\tau^{-1}(H_v) = H_v = \tau(H_v)$, as well as $\theta^s(H_v) = \theta(H_v)$. Assume now that $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. Then on $\{H_v<+\infty\}$ we can compute with the strong Markov property of $W$ as follows \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\comp\theta^s_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\comp\theta_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{align*} It is readily checked that $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\subset\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}$, and therefore we get in particular the strong Markov property of $W^s$ with respect to $H^s_v=H_v$ in the form \begin{equation} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H^s_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\bigr) = P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{equation} Finally, with the strong Markov property of the standard one-dimensional Brownian motions on every edge and the strong Markov property~\eqref{sSMT_v} just proved we can apply the arguments similar to those in~\cite[Section 3.6]{ItMc74} to conclude that $W^s$ is a Feller process. Hence it is strongly Markovian relative to the filtration $\mathcal{F}^s$. By construction, $W^s$ is up to time $H^s_v$ equivalent to a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, and it has continuous sample paths.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Simple Markov property via the time change, strong Markov at $H_v$, then Ito-McKean arguments give the Feller property.

nodes.statement: First we prove the simple Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$. To this end, let $s$, $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. nodes.name: Strong Markov at the vertex hitting time

By construction, $\ensuremath W^s$ and $W$ have the same paths up to the hitting time of the vertex, and in particular $H^s_v$ is also the hitting time of the vertex by $W$, that is, $H^s_v=H_v$. Moreover, since $L^w(H_v)=0$, we get that $\tau^{-1}(H_v) = H_v = \tau(H_v)$, as well as $\theta^s(H_v) = \theta(H_v)$. Then on $\{H_v<+\infty\}$ we can compute with the strong Markov property of $W$ as follows \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\comp\theta^s_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\comp\theta_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{align*} It is readily checked that $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\subset\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}$, and therefore we get in particular the strong Markov property of $W^s$ with respect to $H^s_v=H_v$ in the form \begin{equation} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H^s_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\bigr) = P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: Since $\tau(H_v)=H_v$, strong Markov property at $H^s_v$.

nodes.statement: P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H^s_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\bigr) = P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr).

nodes.statement_short: Ito-McKean arguments give the Feller, hence strong Markov, property.

nodes.name: Path properties
nodes.statement: By construction, $W^s$ is up to time $H^s_v$ equivalent to a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, and it has continuous sample paths.

nodes.statement_short: Before $H^s_v$, $W^s$ is a one-dimensional Brownian motion with continuous paths.

nodes.name: The sticky Walsh process is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement: Hence, altogether we have shown that $\ensuremath W^s$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: $\ensuremath W^s$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}

nodes.name: The vertex is not a trap for $W^s$
nodes.statement: Now we want to compute the generator of $\ensuremath W^s$, and first we argue that $v$ is not a trap for $\ensuremath W^s$. To this end, we may consider $W$ as constructed from a standard Brownian motion $B$ as described in section~\ref{sect2}. Let $Z$ denote the zero set of $B$. Given $s\ge 0$ we can choose $t_0\ge s$ in the complement $Z^c$ of $Z$. Consider $t = \tau^{-1}(t_0)$, i.e., $t = t_0 + \gamma L^w_{t_0}$. Obviously $t\ge s$, and $\tau(t)\in Z^c$. Therefore $B_{\tau(t)} \ne 0$, and consequently $\ensuremath W^s_t=W_{\tau(t)}\ne v$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: For any $s$ pick $t_0\ge s$ off the zero set of $B$; then $W^s$ is away from $v$ at time $\tau^{-1}(t_0)\ge s$.

nodes.name: Generator of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=0$, $c\in(0,1)$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$. Set \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-c},\,\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n,\qquad \gamma = \frac{c}{1-c}, \end{equation} and let $\ensuremath W^s$ be the sticky Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters. Then the generator $A^s$ of $\ensuremath W^s$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\mathcal{G}$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.

nodes.statement_short: With $w_k=b_k/(1-c)$, $\gamma=c/(1-c)$, the sticky Walsh process realizes the boundary condition with $a=0$.
nodes.label: thm4.2

nodes.name: Parameters of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-c},\,\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n,\qquad \gamma = \frac{c}{1-c},
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.4

nodes.name: Exit time $H^s_{v,\epsilon}$ of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon>0$, and let $\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon}$ denote the hitting time of the complement of the open ball $B_\epsilon(v)$ with radius $\epsilon$ and center $v$ by $\ensuremath W^s$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: Let $W$, and therefore also $\ensuremath W^s$, start in the vertex $v$. Since $\ensuremath W^s$ and $W$ have continuous paths with infinite lifetime we have for all $\gamma\ge 0$ \begin{equation*} \ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_{\tau(t)})=\epsilon\bigr\}, \end{equation*} and in particular for $\gamma=0$, \begin{equation*} \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_t)=\epsilon\bigr\}. \end{equation*} Moreover, as argued above, both infima are a.s.\ finite. Set \begin{equation*} \sigma = \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon} + \gamma\,L^w_{\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}}. \end{equation*} Then $\tau(\sigma) = \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$, and therefore \begin{align*} d\bigl(v, \ensuremath W^s_\sigma\bigr) &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\sigma)}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}}\bigr)\\ &= \epsilon. \end{align*} Consequently we get $\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon} \le \sigma$. To derive the converse inequality we remark that \begin{align*} \epsilon &= d\bigl(v, \ensuremath W^s_{\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon}}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon})}\bigr), \end{align*} which implies \begin{equation*} \tau\bigl(\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)\ge \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}. \end{equation*} Since $\tau$ is strictly increasing this entails \begin{equation*} \ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon} \ge \tau^{-1}\bigl(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) = \sigma, \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.

Alternatively, $\ensuremath r^s_\lambda$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \begin{split} \ensuremath r^s_\lambda(\xi,d\eta) = r_\lambda(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\,&\ensuremath S^s_{km}(\lambda)\,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_{\lambda,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} +\gamma\lambda}\,e_\lambda(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $r_\lambda$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and \begin{equation} \ensuremath S^s_{km}(\lambda) = 2\,\frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda}\,w_m - \delta_{km}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Quantum scattering interpretation of the sticky vertex
nodes.statement: When all $w_m$, $m=1$, \dots, $n$, are equal to $1/n$, the matrix $S^s(\lambda)$ takes the form \begin{equation*} S^s(\lambda) = -\1 + \frac{2\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} + \gamma \lambda}\,P_n \end{equation*} which reduces to~\eqref{eq2.6a} when $\gamma=0$. $S^s(\lambda)$ is unitary for all $\lambda<0$. Also the $S^s(\lambda)$ for different $\lambda$ all commute. As a consequence $S^s(\lambda)$ has the interpretation of a quantum scattering matrix in the sense of~\cite{KoSc99}. More precisely, $S^s(\lambda)$ stems from the Schr\"odinger operator $-\Delta^s$, where $\Delta^s$ is a self-adjoint Laplace operator on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ with boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc} with the choice \begin{equation} \begin{split} A &= - \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(S^s(\lambda_0)+\1\bigr),\\ B &= - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\mathstrut2\lambda_0}}\,\bigl(S^s(\lambda_0)-\1\bigr), \end{split} \end{equation} for any $\lambda_0$ for which $\sqrt{2\lambda_0}+\gamma\lambda_0\ne 0$. We emphasize that the Schr\"odinger operator $-\Delta^s$ and the generator $A^s$ of the Walsh process are quite different: Not only do they act on different Banach spaces, but also the functions in the intersection of their domains satisfy different boundary conditions at the vertex $v$. As matter of fact, the integral kernel of the resolvent $(-\Delta^s+2\lambda)^{-1}$ of the Schr\"odinger operator $-\Delta^s$ is given by, see Lemma~4.2 in~\cite{KoSc06}, \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2}\Bigl(r_\lambda(\xi,\eta) +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\, \ensuremath S^s_{km}(\lambda)\,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_{\lambda,m}(\eta)\Bigl), \end{equation*} that is --- up to a factor $2$ --- by the right hand side of~\eqref{eq4.14a} \emph{without} the last term. In more detail and with the definition~\eqref{SE} \begin{equation*} S_{A,B}\bigl(E=-2\lambda\bigr) = S^s(\lambda) \end{equation*} holds for all $\lambda>0$. As a function of $k$ ($k^2=E$), $S^s$ is meromorphic in the complex $k$--plane with a pole on the positive imaginary axis at $k^b=2i/\gamma$. This corresponds to a negative eigenvalue $E^b=-4/\gamma^2$ of $-\Delta^s$. The corresponding (normalized) eigenfunction $\psi^b$ --- physically speaking a \emph{bound state} --- is given as \begin{equation*} \psi^b(\xi) = \frac{1}{2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{n}}\,e^{-2 d(v,\xi)/\gamma},\qquad \xi\in\mathcal{G}. \end{equation*} So quantum mechanically the vertex $v$ acts like an attractive potential. We view this as a quantum analogue of the stickiness of the vertex $v$. This analogy can be elaborated a bit further by inspecting the associated quantum mechanical time delay matrix (see, e.g., \cite{AmJa77, BrFr02, JaMi72, Ma76, Ma81, Na80, Wi55}) \begin{equation*} T(k) = \frac{1}{2ik}\,S(k)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial k} S(k) \end{equation*} which in the present context gives \begin{equation*} T(k) = \frac{-2\gamma}{k(4+k^2\gamma^2)}\,P_n. \end{equation*} So $T(k)$ has zero as an $(n-1)$--fold eigenvalue plus the non-degenerate eigenvalue \begin{equation*} \frac{-2\gamma}{k(4+k^2\gamma^2)}, \end{equation*} which for $\gamma>0$ is the signal for a strict quantum delay. Observe that for $k\to +\infty$, that is for large energies, the time delay experienced by the quantum particle tends to zero, while for $k\to 0$, i.e., for low energies, the delay becomes arbitrarily large. From the physical point of view, both effects are clearly to be expected. For comparison and in contrast to the present stochastic context, in quantum mechanics $\gamma<0$ is also allowed for a meaningful Schr\"odinger operator and an associated scattering matrix.

nodes.name: $L^s$ is the local time of $W^s$ at the vertex
nodes.statement: By construction, $L^s$ is pathwise continuous and non-decreasing. It is adapted to $\mathcal{F}^s$, and a straightforward calculation based on the additivity of $L^w$ and formula~\eqref{eq4.2} shows the (pathwise) additivity property \begin{equation} L^s_{s+t} = L^s_t + L^s_s \comp \theta^s_t,\qquad s,\,t\ge 0. \end{equation} Thus $L^s$ is a PCHAF of $(W^s,\mathcal{F}^s)$. Furthermore, $t\ge 0$ is a point of increase for $L^s$ if only if $\tau(t)$ is a point of increase for $L^w$, which only is the case if $W_{\tau(t)}$ is at the vertex, i.e., if $W^s_t$ is at the vertex. Thus, it follows that $L^s$ is a local time at the vertex for $W^s$. In order to completely identify it, it remains to compute its normalization, and it is not very hard to compute its $\alpha$--potential (the interested reader can find the details for the case $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$ in~\cite{BMMG0}): \begin{equation} E_\xi\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha t}\,dL^s_t\Bigr) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\alpha}+\gamma\alpha}\,e^{-\sqrt{2\alpha}\,d(\xi,v)},\qquad \alpha>0,\,\xi\in\mathcal{G}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.7
nodes.statement: As in the previous cases it is readily seen that the definition~\eqref{eq5.5a} of the parameters $\gamma$, $\beta$, $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, is consistent with the conditions used in the above construction of $\ensuremath W^g$. Let $A^g$ be the generator of $\ensuremath W^g$ with domain $\mathcal{D}(A^g)$. Since $\ensuremath W^g$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}, it follows from theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} that $\mathcal{D}(A^g)\subset \ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$, and that for all $f\in\mathcal{D}(A^g)$, $A^g f(\xi) = 1/2\,f''(\xi)$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$. Let $h\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $\lambda>0$. Then $\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\in\mathcal{D}(A^g)$, and therefore we may compute with equation~\eqref{eq5.4} as follows \begin{align*} \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) &= \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) - \beta\,\rho(\lambda)\,2\lambda \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) - \beta\,\rho(\lambda)\,\gamma\lambda \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v), \end{align*} where we used the fact that, since $\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h$ is in the domain of the generator $A^s$ of $\ensuremath W^s$, it satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq4.7}. We rewrite this equation in the following way: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) &+\beta\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\rho(\lambda) \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v)\\ &-\beta\,\rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda\bigr)\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\Bigr)(v). \end{split} \end{equation} Now we differentiate equation~\eqref{eq5.4} at $\xi\in l_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, let $\xi$ tend to $v$ along any edge $l_k$, and sum the resulting equation against the weights $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$. Then we get the following formula \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) + \beta\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v), \end{equation} where we used $\sum_k w_k=1$. On the other hand, for $\xi=v$, equation~\eqref{eq5.4} gives \begin{equation} \bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)(v) = \rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} +\gamma\lambda\bigr)\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v). \end{equation} A comparison of equations~\eqref{eq5.6}, \eqref{eq5.7} with \eqref{eq5.5} shows that we have proved the following formula \begin{equation} \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) - \beta \bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)(v). \end{equation} With the values~\eqref{eq5.5a} for $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, it is obvious that $f=\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h$ satisfies equation~\eqref{eq1.1b}. Since $\ensuremath R^g_\lambda$ is surjective from $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ onto the domain of the generator $A^g$ of $\ensuremath W^g$, the proof of the theorem is finished.
